title: Disk and network health
lead: When a server slows down, check two things first: disk usage and the network. Do a quick health check with df, du, free, uptime, ip, ping and ss.
objectives: Find which partition is full with `df -h` and which folder takes the space with `du`.
Read memory and load with `free -h` and `uptime`.
Narrow down a network problem layer by layer with `ip`, `ping` and `ss`.
Save health output to a file and prepare a report for a support ticket.

sections.title: Disk usage: df and du
body: When a disk hits 100%, writes fail with `No space left on device`; services and logs stop. So first ask **which partition** is full: `df -h`. Columns: `Size` total, `Used`, `Avail` free, `Use%` percentage, `Mounted on` the mount point.

Once you know the partition, find **which folder** uses the space with `du`. `du -sh folder` gives a total; `du -h --max-depth=1 folder | sort -h` lists subfolders from small to large. Sometimes space looks free but files cannot be created: inodes ran out, check with `df -i`.

commands.what: Shows size and usage of partitions in readable units.
commands.where: First command on slowness or 'disk full' errors.
commands.why: Shows at a glance which mount point has the problem.

commands.what: Shows the total size of a folder.
commands.where: After df shows the full partition.

commands.what: Lists sizes of folders one level down; sort with sort -h.
commands.why: Drills down without walking the whole tree.

commands.where: Space is free but files cannot be created.
commands.why: Millions of tiny files can exhaust inodes.

sections.tip: `df` finds the partition, `du` finds the folder. Do df first, then du.
sections.warn: Check what a file is with `ls -l` before deleting. For a log of a running service, truncating it (`: > file`) is often better than deleting; if unsure, ask your administrator.

sections.title: Memory and load: free and uptime
body: `free -h` shows RAM and swap. Watch the `available` column: memory that can really be given to new programs. Even if `free` looks small, cache (`buff/cache`) is released when needed, so do not panic.
`uptime` shows how long the system has been up and the **load average** (1, 5, 15 minutes). If load constantly exceeds your CPU core count, work is queuing up.

commands.what: Shows RAM and swap usage in readable units.
commands.why: available tells the real free memory.

commands.what: Shows uptime, user count and load average.
commands.where: Quick check on a slow server.
commands.why: Load average shows a trend, not a snapshot.

sections.tip: To make a report, use `df -h > report.txt`, and `>>` to append.

sections.title: Network: ip, ping and ss
body: Narrow a network problem from the bottom up: 1) Is the interface up and does it have an IP? `ip -br a`. 2) Is there a default route (gateway)? `ip route`. 3) Is the gateway reachable? `ping -c 3 <gateway>`. 4) An internet IP? `ping -c 3 1.1.1.1`. 5) Name resolution? `ping -c 3 example.com`.

If ping works for an IP but not for a name, the problem is **DNS** (`/etc/resolv.conf`). If nothing works, check the cable, VM network setting or gateway. `ss -tuln` shows which ports the machine listens on (e.g. 22 for SSH).

commands.what: Lists interfaces, their state and IP addresses briefly.
commands.where: First step in a network problem.
commands.why: Without an IP there is no point checking higher layers.

commands.what: Shows the routing table and default gateway.
commands.where: When you cannot reach the outside.
commands.why: Without a default via line, traffic cannot leave.

commands.what: Sends 3 test packets to a target; reports loss and latency.

commands.where: To see if a service listens on its port.
commands.why: Checks the server side of 'I cannot connect'.

sections.danger: On a remote server, commands like `ip link set eth0 down` cut your SSH connection and lock you out. Make sure you have console access before changing network settings.

t04.text: Read the sample report `~/reports/df_sample.txt` with `cat` and find the Use% column.

t05.text: Save the output of `df -h` to `~/disk_report.txt` with `>`.

t06.text: Append the output of `free -h` to the same file (`>>`).
t06.hint: `>>` appends, `>` overwrites; if you overwrote it, repeat t05.

t07.text: Append the output of `uptime` to `~/disk_report.txt` too.

t08.text: Predict: which mount point is the line with 95% in `~/reports/df_sample.txt`? Then verify with `grep 95% ~/reports/df_sample.txt`.
t08.hint: The Mounted on column at the end of the line.

t09.text: Predict: what does `~/reports/ping_sample.txt` say about the network? See the loss rate with `grep loss ~/reports/ping_sample.txt`.
t09.hint: 100% packet loss means the target was never reached.

t10.text: Predict: what is the IP of interface eth0 in `~/reports/ip_sample.txt`? Verify with `grep eth0 ~/reports/ip_sample.txt`.
t10.hint: The /24 is the netmask, not part of the IP.

t11.text: The disk is bloating. Look with `ls -l ~/logs`; the old debug log `old_debug.log` is useless, delete it but do not touch `app.log`.
t11.hint: `rm ~/logs/old_debug.log`. Check the exact name with ls before deleting.

t12.text: Mini project: build the report `~/health.txt`. It should contain, in order, the heading `== disk ==`, the `df -h` output, the heading `== memory ==` and the `free -h` output.
t12.hint: First line `echo "== disk ==" > ~/health.txt`, the rest with `>>`.

t13.text: Challenge: from `~/reports/df_sample.txt` write only the 95% line to `~/alert.txt` and the number of such lines to `~/alert_count.txt`.
t13.hint: `grep` filters the line, `grep -c` counts; redirect both with `>`.

t14.text: Ticket: "The application throws 'No space left on device'." Find the full mount point in `~/reports/df_sample.txt` and write its name to `~/full_mount.txt`. Also delete the useless `~/logs/core.dump`.
t14.hint: The full one is the 95% line. The mount point is `/var`: `echo /var > ~/full_mount.txt`.

vm.intro: The commands here only read information, so they are safe on your VM. Paste the output and we will check it automatically.

v01.title: Disk usage
v01.text: Run `df -h` and paste the output. Note the usage percentage of the root (`/`) partition.

blocks.expected:
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda2        19G  4.1G   14G  23% /

differs: The partition may be `/dev/vda1`, `/dev/mapper/...` or `/dev/nvme0n1p2`; the Use% column is what matters.
Many `tmpfs`/`loop` lines are normal (Ubuntu snap); focus on the `/` line.

v02.title: Space hunt
v02.text: Sort the sizes of your home directory and of the folders under /var. Paste the largest 5 lines.
differs: If `sort -h` is missing (very old system) use `sort -n` and `du -k`.
If sudo asks for a password, enter your VM user password; it is not shown while typing.

v03.title: IP and routing
v03.text: Show your interfaces and default gateway; paste the output.

blocks.expected:
lo      UNKNOWN  127.0.0.1/8
enp0s3  UP       10.0.2.15/24
default via 10.0.2.2 dev enp0s3

differs: The interface name may be `eth0`, `enp0s3` or `ens160`.
On VirtualBox NAT the IP is usually 10.0.2.15; with bridged networking it comes from your router's range.
If there is no IP at all, check that the VM network card is connected and set to NAT/Bridged.

v04.title: Connectivity and DNS test
v04.text: Ping an IP first, then a name. Paste both outputs.
differs: If the IP works but the name does not, it is a DNS problem; look at `cat /etc/resolv.conf`.
Some networks block ICMP; if ping fails but the web works, the problem is ping itself.

v05.title: Listening ports
v05.text: List the ports your machine listens on and paste the output.
differs: If SSH is not installed, 22 will not appear; that is fine for this module.
If `ss` is missing, try `netstat -tuln` on old systems.

q1.q: Which command shows which partition is full?
q1.explain: `df` shows partition usage, `du` shows folder sizes.

q2.q: `/var` is 95% full. How do you find the biggest subfolder?
q2.explain: du gives subfolder sizes, sort -h orders them small to large.

q3.q: `ping 1.1.1.1` works but `ping example.com` does not. Most likely problem?
q3.explain: The IP is reachable but names are not resolved: check DNS settings.

q4.q: Which command shows the ports the machine listens on?

summary: `df -h` answers which partition, `du -sh` / `du --max-depth=1` which folder is full.
In `free -h` watch `available`; in `uptime` the load average.
Narrow network problems bottom-up: `ip -br a`, `ip route`, ping an IP, ping a name.
Turn output into a report with `>` and `>>`; check with `ls -l` before deleting.

glossary.meaning: A record holding information about a file; their number is limited.

The exit from the local network to the outside (usually the router).
